title: Ephemeral sessions get context via the curated shared tier, never raw memory
body: Raw transcript memory stays local by design (E2E-encrypted when synced between own machines) and is never shipped into ephemeral/web sandboxes: a private brain plus passphrase handling do not belong in a shared environment. The supported channel into ephemeral sessions and to teammates is this curated tier (.kit/shared/memory.jsonl) plus the repo CLAUDE.md. Closing the ephemeral-context gap therefore means feeding this tier at arc boundaries, not building new sync infrastructure.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Public-repo promote policy: publicity-tolerant entries only, landed via PR
body: Every entry in this file is world-readable the moment it merges. Promote only what tolerates publicity: decisions with their why, conventions, abandoned paths with reasons, unbuilt ideas. Security findings, customer details, and internal reasoning about third parties go to the private research repo, never here. No session URLs or internal metadata (same hygiene as issues/PRs). Entries land via PR review, never a direct push to the default branch, and the file is append-only: supersede or reverse an entry instead of editing it.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: 6.3.2 is the release that MEASURES the attestation fix — docs stay caveated until it verifies
body: The GitHub artifact attestation errored in 327 ms on every kit release before 6.3.2 (subject-path dist/**/* = 1920 files vs the action's 1024-subject limit) and continue-on-error reported it to the jobs API as success. The fix packs the tarball and attests that single subject. Deliberate sequencing: docs/VERIFY.md keeps its caveat and the CI snippet keeps the attestation gate non-blocking (|| echo ::warning::) UNTIL gh attestation verify actually answers for 6.3.2. Removing them on the strength of an unrun fix is the exact failure the arc exists to correct — a check that could not run, reported as one that passed.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Prove a pinned CI secret from the run log, not by reading it
body: GitHub never exposes a secret's value, so 'is MAINTAINER_KEY_FPR the right fingerprint?' looks unanswerable from a workstation. It is not: the publish workflow's 'Import maintainer public key' step exits non-zero unless the imported key's fingerprint equals the secret exactly, and the imported key is the one committed at the verified tag. So a SUCCEEDING step plus the tag's own pubkey pins the secret's value transitively. Measured for 6.3.1 (run 30804371457): the log line reads 'Maintainer key fingerprint matches the pinned secret (single key in keyring)' and the pubkey at v6.3.1 is F6BBD5CDAFA615C51F43D73206EA76F88AC0482A. Generalise: when a gate compares a secret to something public and fails closed, a green run is a measurement of the secret.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A broken instruction can hide behind a true caveat — gate the command, not just the claim
body: docs/VERIFY.md shipped 'gh attestation verify --owner sandstream --repo kit <tarball>', which exits 1 (the flags are alternatives; --repo wants owner/repo). It survived review because the caveat directly above it truthfully said the attestation did not exist yet, so nobody expected the command to succeed. The caveat was accurate AND it camouflaged a defect in the same paragraph. Generalisation: when a doc hedges that something is unavailable, the instructions under that hedge stop being exercised — audit them at the moment the hedge is removed, and prefer an offline grammar gate over a fix. src/docs-verify-commands.test.ts does this for VERIFY.md/README/publish.yml; it deliberately avoids network so it cannot be skipped in CI, and asserts at least one invocation exists so deletion cannot make it vacuously green.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: The plugin policy channel carries the DECISION, not the config
body: kit-plugin-* packages must not import kit-core (adapter-sdk: monorepo coupling + private-package leaks), so [policy.agent_writes] cannot be enforced by a kit function call. Chosen: kit resolves every POLICY_OPS entry through the single policyDecision and exports only the refusals as KIT_POLICY_DENY (vendor:op, comma-separated). The plugin guard is then a membership test with NO rule in it. Rejected: serialising the config into the env and letting each plugin apply the four-state rule — that puts seven independent implementations of one access rule in seven packages, and each could collapse trap 1 (empty list = lock) or trap 2 (absent vendor != empty) on its own. Absence of the var must mean 'no denial', never 'denied', or every inert repo goes offline when a plugin runs outside a kit invocation. Two limits to keep stating: the channel is exactly as strong as KIT_READ_ONLY and no stronger, and a plugin-side refusal is NOT audited (a plugin has no path to the governed project's log).
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A fix inside packages/ does not ship until its package.json version is bumped
body: publish.yml's publish_ws skips any workspace whose version already exists on npm ('already on npm — skipping'). So a behaviour change in a kit-plugin-* package with an unchanged version lands in the monorepo and leaves every installed copy unchanged — silently, with a green publish run. This bit the containment fix for the plugin write surfaces: without bumping the seven touched plugins to 0.1.1, the read-only and policy guards would have existed only for people who cloned the repo. Treat a version bump as part of any packages/ fix, and remember the same shape as the pre-6.3.1 state where the scanner plugins existed but were unreachable to anyone who had not cloned.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A convention-enforced guard needs a test that derives the surfaces from source
body: kit-plugin-supabase shipped three write surfaces with no read-only guard while six sibling plugins had one, and four documents claimed 'every kit-plugin write surface' was covered. Nothing could catch it: the guard was a convention, and a convention is enforced by whoever remembers it. The gate that works (src/plugin-write-gates.test.ts) derives the surfaces from the plugin SOURCES rather than a maintained list — every function issuing a mutating request must appear in an expected mapping with both guards, in order, naming a registered op. Two details that matter: pin the MAPPING not just the presence (gating a token-revoke on env_set would satisfy a presence check), and add a second detector for writes routed through a shared transport (a GraphQL mutation's POST lives in the transport, so exempting the transport would exempt every future write through it). Exemptions carry written reasons and are asserted to still match something, so a rename cannot leave a stale grant behind.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: A limitation recorded without its condition reads as permanent
body: The ROADMAP parked an upstream issue as unfileable: 'any repository outside the allowlist answers 403, so a human has to open it.' Measured when the item finally came up: gh issue list against that repo exits 0. The 403 was real but belonged to a DIFFERENT constraint — a cloud session's GitHub token is scoped to its one attached repo — and had been copied onto a local-session item where it never applied. Effect: an actionable item sat recorded as impossible, and the note was quoted forward through three session summaries without anyone re-testing it. Rule: when recording a blocker, record the CONDITION it depends on (which surface, which session type, which credential), and re-measure a one-line check before repeating the claim. A blocker without its condition is indistinguishable from a permanent one.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Drafted upstream issue dropped — the ask already existed, so evidence went to the open thread
body: ROADMAP carried a ready-to-file draft asking modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk to move its HTTP/OAuth deps to optionalDependencies. Searching upstream first found typescript-sdk#1924, open since 2026-04-17, asking the same thing with the same three options and two supporters. Filing the draft would have been a third +1. What was contributed instead: the measurement nobody in the thread had — which packages actually EXECUTE (9 of 94 load; all twelve HTTP/OAuth packages installed, none loaded), the method caveat (an ESM-only tracer misses ajv's internal require of fast-uri and under-reports by half), and the argument that beats disk footprint: of three advisories cleared from that subtree, two were unreachable and one (fast-uri via ajv) was genuinely live, and only a runtime trace tells them apart. Generalise: before filing a drafted issue, search the target repo — a duplicate spends the maintainer's attention and buries the thread that already has traction, whereas evidence added to the existing thread compounds. Prefer the measurement the thread lacks over restating its premise.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>

title: Never pipe a release gate's output through tail — the one run that matters is the one you then cannot read
body: Cutting 6.4.0, a full-suite run on the release branch reported '# fail 1'. The command was 'npm test 2>&1 | tail -8', so everything above the summary was discarded and the failing test's NAME was gone. Four subsequent full runs were green (4012/4012 each), so the flake could not be reproduced and remains unidentified. Cost: a known-flaky test in a release gate with no way to name it, which is exactly the shape that teaches people to re-run until green. Rule: capture a gate run to a FILE (npm test > run.log 2>&1) and read the summary from the file, so a failure keeps its detail. Related trap hit in the same session: 'cmd | tail; echo 0' reports tail's exit code, not cmd's — an attestation verify looked like it passed on an empty output until the exit code was read without the pipe. Both are the same error: putting a pipe between a measurement and its evidence.
author: Peter Sandström <peter@sandstre.am>
